question: Does complying with the Navigation Rules excuse a vessel, its owner, or its operator from the consequences of neglecting a precaution required by ordinary practice of seamen or by the special circumstances of a case?
choice_a: Yes, following the Rules is a complete legal defense in any collision
choice_b: Only if the neglect happened while operating in a narrow channel
choice_c: No -- the Rules do not excuse any neglect of a precaution required by the ordinary practice of seamen or by the special circumstances of the case
choice_d: Only if the other vessel involved was also violating the Rules
explanation: Nothing in the Rules exonerates any vessel, owner, or crew from the consequences of neglecting any precaution required by ordinary seamanship or by the special circumstances of the case.

question: Per the Navigation Rules, when may an operator depart from the literal steering and sailing rules?
choice_a: Never -- the Rules must be followed exactly no matter the circumstances
choice_b: Only with prior radio clearance from another vessel
choice_c: Only during an organized boat race or regatta
choice_d: When necessary to avoid immediate danger, giving due regard to the dangers of navigation, collision, and any special circumstances including the limitations of the vessels involved
explanation: In construing and complying with the Rules, due regard must be had to all dangers of navigation and collision and to any special circumstances, including vessel limitations, which may make a departure from the Rules necessary to avoid immediate danger.

question: Under the Navigation Rules' definitions, what is a "power-driven vessel"?
choice_a: Any vessel propelled by machinery
choice_b: Any vessel with more than 10 horsepower installed
choice_c: Any vessel that can be sailed but currently has its sails lowered
choice_d: Any vessel operating faster than idle speed
explanation: The Navigation Rules define "power-driven vessel" simply as any vessel propelled by machinery.

question: Under the Navigation Rules, when does a vessel with sails count as a "sailing vessel" for right-of-way purposes?
choice_a: Whenever it has sails rigged, even if its engine is also running
choice_b: When it is under sail and any propelling machinery it has fitted is not being used
choice_c: Only when it is registered with the state as a sailboat
choice_d: Only when it has no engine installed at all
explanation: "Sailing vessel" means any vessel under sail, provided that propelling machinery, if fitted, is not being used -- a sailboat motoring under power is legally a power-driven vessel.

question: Under the Navigation Rules' definitions, does a recreational angler trolling a fishing line from a moving boat count as a "vessel engaged in fishing" with special right-of-way status?
choice_a: Yes, any boat with a fishing line in the water automatically qualifies
choice_b: Yes, but only if the boat is anchored while fishing
choice_c: No -- "vessel engaged in fishing" means fishing with nets, lines, trawls, or other apparatus that restricts maneuverability, and specifically excludes trolling lines or gear that do not restrict maneuverability
choice_d: No such exception exists -- all fishing boats have the same status
explanation: "Vessel engaged in fishing" means a vessel fishing with nets, lines, trawls, or other apparatus which restricts maneuverability, but does not include a vessel fishing with trolling lines or other gear that does not restrict maneuverability.

question: Under the Navigation Rules' definitions, what is a vessel "restricted in her ability to maneuver"?
choice_a: Any vessel that has lost engine power entirely
choice_b: Any vessel operating at idle speed in a no-wake zone
choice_c: A vessel that is legally overloaded beyond its capacity plate
choice_d: A vessel which, from the nature of her work, is restricted in her ability to maneuver as required by the Rules and is therefore unable to keep out of the way of another vessel
explanation: A vessel "restricted in her ability to maneuver" is one which, from the nature of her work, is restricted in her ability to maneuver as required by the Rules and is therefore unable to keep out of the way of another vessel -- a different status than a "vessel not under command."

question: The steering and sailing rules governing crossing, overtaking, and head-on situations (right-of-way between two boats) apply under what condition?
choice_a: Only when the vessels are in sight of one another, meaning each can be observed visually from the other
choice_b: Only when both vessels are equipped with radar
choice_c: At all times, including when vessels are hidden from each other by fog or a bend in the shoreline
choice_d: Only during daylight hours
explanation: The right-of-way rules for vessels in sight of one another (such as crossing, overtaking, and head-on) apply only when the vessels can be observed visually from one another; different rules govern conduct in restricted visibility.

question: When determining whether risk of collision exists, what does the Navigation Rules say about assumptions based on scanty radar information?
choice_a: A single radar contact is always sufficient to rule out risk of collision
choice_b: Assumptions shall not be made on the basis of scanty information, especially scanty radar information
choice_c: Radar information should be ignored in favor of visual observation alone
choice_d: Scanty radar information should be treated as proof that no risk exists
explanation: The Rules specifically caution that assumptions about risk of collision shall not be made on the basis of scanty information, especially scanty radar information.

question: If the compass bearing of an approaching vessel does not appreciably change over time, what must an operator assume?
choice_a: The other vessel is standing still and poses no threat
choice_b: The vessels will safely pass close aboard with no action needed
choice_c: Risk of collision shall be deemed to exist
choice_d: Nothing can be determined without radar
explanation: Risk of collision shall be deemed to exist if the compass bearing of an approaching vessel does not appreciably change -- a steady, unchanging bearing signals a collision course.

question: Can risk of collision exist even when the compass bearing of an approaching vessel IS changing appreciably?
choice_a: No, an appreciably changing bearing always means the vessels will safely pass
choice_b: No, bearing changes only matter for sailing vessels
choice_c: Yes, but only in a narrow channel
choice_d: Yes -- risk may still exist, particularly when approaching a very large vessel, a tow, or another vessel at close range
explanation: Risk of collision may sometimes exist even when an appreciable bearing change is evident, particularly when approaching a very large vessel, a tow, or a vessel at close range.

question: What does the Navigation Rules say about a succession of small course or speed alterations when trying to avoid a collision?
choice_a: Any alteration should be large enough to be readily apparent to another vessel, and a succession of small alterations should be avoided
choice_b: A succession of small alterations is always preferred over one large alteration
choice_c: Small alterations are required by law in every situation
choice_d: Course alterations are prohibited; only speed changes are permitted
explanation: Any alteration of course and/or speed to avoid collision shall, circumstances admitting, be large enough to be readily apparent to another vessel observing visually or by radar; a succession of small alterations should be avoided.

question: If there is sufficient sea room, what may be the most effective single action to avoid a close-quarters situation?
choice_a: Sounding the horn continuously instead of maneuvering
choice_b: Alteration of course alone, made in good time and substantial, provided it does not create another close-quarters situation
choice_c: Increasing speed to clear the area faster
choice_d: Turning off all navigation lights to avoid being seen
explanation: If there is sufficient sea room, alteration of course alone may be the most effective action to avoid a close-quarters situation, provided it is made in good time, is substantial, and does not result in another close-quarters situation.

question: After taking action to avoid a collision, what is an operator required to do?
choice_a: Nothing further -- the initial action satisfies the operator's full duty
choice_b: Immediately resume the original course regardless of the other vessel's position
choice_c: Carefully check the effectiveness of the action until the other vessel is finally past and clear
choice_d: Notify the Ohio Department of Natural Resources by radio
explanation: Action taken to avoid collision shall result in passing at a safe distance, and its effectiveness shall be carefully checked until the other vessel is finally past and clear.

question: If necessary to avoid collision or to allow more time to assess a situation, what may a vessel be required to do with its speed?
choice_a: Increase speed immediately to clear the danger area
choice_b: Maintain exactly the same speed no matter what
choice_c: Shift into neutral only, never reverse
choice_d: Slacken her speed or take all way off by stopping or reversing her means of propulsion
explanation: If necessary to avoid collision or to allow more time to assess the situation, a vessel shall slacken her speed or take all way off by stopping or reversing her means of propulsion.

question: Per the Navigation Rules, should a vessel anchor in a narrow channel?
choice_a: Any vessel shall, if the circumstances of the case admit, avoid anchoring in a narrow channel
choice_b: Anchoring in a narrow channel is always permitted for vessels under 20 feet
choice_c: Anchoring in a narrow channel is required whenever another vessel is overtaking
choice_d: There is no rule addressing anchoring location
explanation: Any vessel shall, if the circumstances of the case admit, avoid anchoring in a narrow channel, since an anchored vessel there can obstruct other traffic that can navigate safely only within the channel.

question: A sailing vessel has the wind on her port side and sees another sailing vessel to windward, but cannot determine with certainty which side the other vessel has the wind on. What must the first vessel do?
choice_a: Hold course and speed and require the other vessel to give way
choice_b: Keep out of the way of the other vessel
choice_c: Sound five short blasts and continue on course
choice_d: Assume the other vessel also has the wind on her port side
explanation: If a vessel with the wind on the port side sees a vessel to windward and cannot determine with certainty whether the other vessel has the wind on the port or starboard side, she shall keep out of the way of the other.

question: Per the Navigation Rules' definition of overtaking, a vessel is considered to be overtaking another when approaching from what direction?
choice_a: From any direction ahead of the other vessel's beam
choice_b: Directly from astern only, at exactly 180 degrees
choice_c: From a direction more than 22.5 degrees abaft the other vessel's beam -- a position from which, at night, only her sternlight (not her sidelights) would be visible
choice_d: From either side, as long as the vessels are on parallel courses
explanation: A vessel is deemed to be overtaking when coming up on another vessel from a direction more than 22.5 degrees abaft her beam -- a position from which, at night, only the sternlight (and not the sidelights) of the vessel ahead would be seen.

question: If a vessel operator is in doubt as to whether they are overtaking another vessel, what must they do?
choice_a: Assume it is a crossing situation instead
choice_b: Assume no special right-of-way rule applies
choice_c: Radio the other vessel to ask before taking any action
choice_d: Assume that they are overtaking and act accordingly, keeping out of the way of the other vessel
explanation: When a vessel is in any doubt as to whether she is overtaking another, she shall assume that this is the case and act accordingly, keeping out of the way of the vessel ahead.

question: During an overtaking maneuver, if the bearing between the two vessels subsequently changes, does the overtaking vessel become a "crossing" vessel and lose its give-way obligation?
choice_a: No -- a subsequent change of bearing does not make the overtaking vessel a crossing vessel, nor does it relieve her of the duty to keep clear until finally past and clear
choice_b: Yes, any bearing change immediately converts it into a crossing situation under Rule 15
choice_c: Yes, but only if the bearing change exceeds 45 degrees
choice_d: The overtaking vessel's obligation ends as soon as her bow passes the other vessel's stern
explanation: A subsequent alteration of bearing between the two vessels does not make the overtaking vessel a crossing vessel, nor does it relieve her of the duty to keep clear until she is finally past and clear.

question: By day, when is a head-on situation deemed to exist between two power-driven vessels, apart from the nighttime lights test?
choice_a: Only when the two vessels are within 100 feet of each other
choice_b: When a vessel sees the other ahead or nearly ahead and observes the corresponding aspect of the other vessel
choice_c: Head-on situations can only be identified using running lights, never by day
choice_d: Only when both vessels are traveling at their maximum hull speed
explanation: A head-on situation exists when a vessel sees the other ahead or nearly ahead; by day this is judged by observing the corresponding aspect of the other vessel (bow-on), and by night by the alignment of masthead lights and/or sidelights.

question: If an operator is in doubt as to whether a head-on situation exists with another power-driven vessel, what must they assume?
choice_a: That no head-on situation exists unless the other vessel sounds a signal
choice_b: That it must be an overtaking situation instead
choice_c: That a head-on situation does exist, and act accordingly by altering course to starboard
choice_d: Doubt cannot arise once both vessels are visible to each other
explanation: When a vessel is in any doubt as to whether a head-on situation exists, she shall assume that it does exist and act accordingly.

question: May a stand-on vessel take action to avoid collision on her own, before the situation becomes a last-resort emergency?
choice_a: No, the stand-on vessel must hold course and speed no matter what until a collision is imminent
choice_b: No, only the give-way vessel is ever permitted to maneuver
choice_c: Yes, but only by sounding the horn, never by maneuvering
choice_d: Yes -- as soon as it becomes apparent that the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action, the stand-on vessel may take action to avoid collision by her own maneuver alone
explanation: As soon as it becomes apparent to the stand-on vessel that the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action, the stand-on vessel may take action to avoid collision by her maneuver alone.

question: If the stand-on vessel finds herself so close to another vessel that collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel's action alone, what must she do?
choice_a: Take whatever action will best aid to avoid collision
choice_b: Continue holding course and speed regardless, since she is the stand-on vessel
choice_c: Immediately stop her engine and drift
choice_d: Sound one prolonged blast and take no further action
explanation: When the vessel required to keep her course and speed finds herself so close that collision cannot be avoided by the action of the give-way vessel alone, she shall take whatever action will best aid to avoid collision.

question: Does the stand-on vessel rule ever relieve the give-way vessel of her obligation to keep out of the way?
choice_a: Yes, once the stand-on vessel maneuvers, the give-way vessel has no further duty
choice_b: No -- the stand-on vessel rule does not relieve the give-way vessel of her obligation to keep out of the way
choice_c: Yes, but only in a narrow channel
choice_d: The give-way vessel's obligation ends the moment risk of collision is identified
explanation: The stand-on vessel provisions do not relieve the give-way vessel of her obligation to keep out of the way; that duty continues throughout the encounter.

question: Under the responsibilities between vessels, in addition to a sailing vessel, which other vessel must a power-driven vessel underway keep out of the way of?
choice_a: Another power-driven vessel underway in open water with no crossing risk
choice_b: A personal watercraft operating at idle speed
choice_c: A vessel not under command
choice_d: A vessel that is properly anchored outside a channel
explanation: A power-driven vessel underway shall keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, a vessel engaged in fishing, and a sailing vessel.

question: Under the responsibilities between vessels, in addition to a vessel engaged in fishing, a sailing vessel underway must keep out of the way of which other vessel?
choice_a: Any power-driven vessel with no special status
choice_b: A vessel properly anchored in open water
choice_c: A personal watercraft
choice_d: A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver
explanation: A sailing vessel underway shall keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, and a vessel engaged in fishing.

question: Under the responsibilities between vessels, what must a vessel engaged in fishing do when underway, so far as possible?
choice_a: Keep out of the way of a vessel not under command and a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver
choice_b: Hold the right-of-way over every other vessel category without exception
choice_c: Keep out of the way of every sailing vessel it encounters
choice_d: Anchor immediately whenever another vessel approaches
explanation: A vessel engaged in fishing, when underway, shall so far as possible keep out of the way of a vessel not under command and a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver.
